For polytherapy, those regimens containing valproate had a significantly higher risk of major congenital malforma- tions than valproate-free combinations. For monotherapy a relationship between malformations and dose was seen for lamotrigine and although the trend with valproate dos- age did not reach statistical significance infants exposed to more than 1000 mg valproate daily had the highest rate of malformations for any monotherapy. The authors also noted that for lamotrigine the risk with doses more than 200 mg daily was no different to that associated with 1000 mg or less of valproate daily. There is evidence that antiepileptic therapy is associated with lower birth-weight at term, presumably due to drug- induced intra-uterine growth retardation; the effect may be seen largely in women taking multiple antiepilep- tic drugs.7 Additional problems that may occur in the immediate post-partum period include the potential for neonatal seda- tion and dependence with drugs such as phenobarbital or benzodiazepines, if given close to term. Evidence of with- drawal symptoms has also been reported in infants ex- posed to sodium valproate or phenytoin. Some antiepilep- tics induce hepatic enzymes and may also increase the risk of vitamin K deficiency and neonatal bleeding.6,7 There is also increasing concern about the possibility of long-term impairment of neurodevelopment in children exposed to antiepileptic drugs in utero.5,7,10,11,24,25 A pop- ulation-based cohort study26 in young men with epileptic mothers found lower IQ scores and shorter adult heights than in those born to mothers without epilepsy, although information on fetal exposure to individual antiepileptic drugs was unavailable. Again, most evidence implicates valproate;7,10,11 some consider that there is also evidence for phenytoin and carbamazepine,7,10,11 and perhaps phe- nobarbital,10 although a systematic review could not find evidence to implicate any individual antiepileptic,24 and a study involving 182 children exposed to carbamazepine monotherapy could not find evidence of a reduction in ver- bal and nonverbal IQ scores.27 Patients with epilepsy should be offered pre-conception advice and treatment should be individualised.1,3,4,6,7 Women should be advised to plan their pregnancies, and informed of the potential risks of seizures to mother and baby as well as the risks of antiepileptics;7 fatalities have been associated with the mother stopping her antiepileptic regimen inappropriately.5 It should be borne in mind that some antiepileptics may reduce the effectiveness of oral contraception and increase the risk of unplanned pregnan- cy.6,11 Equally, there is some evidence that a degree of sex- ual dysfunction and impaired fertility may occur in both women6,11 and
